UKMTO says five percent of ships attacked since 17 Aug sunk or lost
About 5 percent of vessels reported attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz have been confirmed lost or sunk since the Iran-US Memorandum of Understanding expired on 17 August, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).
Roughly 43 percent of ships in these incidents appear on the non-compliance list of the Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA), which was set up by Iran in May, UKMTO said in its weekly overview.
The PGSA blacklists ships it accuses of breaking its Hormuz transit rules, threatening fines, detention or confiscation. Its list passed 120 vessels in October.
According to the weekly overview, three tankers were struck by unknown projectiles within about 17 minutes on 22 November while heading east through the Strait of Hormuz. All three continued their voyages.
UKMTO documented 10 incidents in the week to 25 November, seven of them in the Strait of Hormuz.
Combined transits remain roughly 65 percent below pre-conflict levels, with 166 outbound and 173 inbound crossings last week. About 70 percent were energy carriers, and more vessels are using the southern route.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has rejected a new request from military chief of staff Eyal Zamir to authorise administrative detention orders against Israeli settlers involved in attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, Kan reported.
Zamir told Katz at a security consultation on Thursday that further steps were needed amid rising settler violence, and called for administrative detention and restraining orders against perpetrators, the report said.
Administrative detention allows suspects to be held indefinitely without charge or trial. It is widely used against Palestinians, including children, but Katz halted its use against Jewish Israelis in November 2024. He has, in fact, repeatedly boasted of doing so, while expanding its use against Palestinians.
Dozens of restraining orders, which bar individuals from parts of the West Bank, are awaiting Shin Bet approval, according to Kan. Channel 12 reported that 70 people suspected of involvement in such attacks were arrested in recent weeks, but Israeli courts released all of them without indictments.
Shin Bet chief David Zini, who belongs to the Orthodox nationalist Hardal camp, has consistently objected to movement bans. He has been accused of undermining the agency's unit tasked with tackling settler violence.

It may also open the door for further violations of rights and freedoms," she added.
Technicality
Oftentimes rulings by the highest court come down to technicalities.
What the court was looking at in this case was the application of Section 33 of the constitution, known as the "notwithstanding clause", which shields Bill 21 from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms itself.

A 30-second advert highlighting US taxpayer funding for Israel was broadcast across the United States on Wednesday night during a Thanksgiving special edition of the long-running sketch show Saturday Night Live.
The ad, from the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project (Imeu), a pro-Palestinian advocacy group based in California, shows an American girl carrying out chores over the course of the year in order to make $400 to buy a new bicycle.
The footage then cuts from the American on a pristine suburban street to a Palestinian girl amid the rubble of Gaza. The Palestinian girl has lost a leg to Israeli bombs and is on crutches.
“Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to Israel to do this,” says the ad's American narrator, against the backdrop of the girl in Gaza.
The US currently officially gives Israel $3.8bn a year, in a 10-year memorandum of understanding that runs from 2019 to 2028, working out at just over $360 every three seconds.

The US currently officially gives Israel $3.8bn a year, in a 10-year memorandum of understanding that runs from 2019 to 2028, working out at just over $360 every three seconds.

Yemen, where civil war broke out in 2014, has recently been rocked by the worst fighting in years. A truce agreed in 2022 between the Ansar Allah, better known as the Houthis, who control the north, and forces loyal to the government in the south disintegrated when Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport in July.
In August and September, the Houthis mounted a quick offensive, recapturing much of the western coast, including the port of Mocha, putting it within close range of ships passing the strategically important Bab el-Mandab strait.
The Houthis are now targeting Aden, Yemen’s second city and seat of its internationally recognised government since the group took the capital Sanaa 12 years ago.
Meanwhile, the Houthis have tightened their decade-long siege of Taiz, blocking the road to Aden and raising the prospect of its capture.
The Saudi-backed pro-government military coalition contains a variety of armed units and local militias, each with different goals, rival leaders and origins, leading to infighting and disorganisation.
Allegiances frequently shift and evolve: the Giants Brigade and the National Resistance Forces were each previously backed by the UAE. The leaders of both, like much of the coalition, are now bankrolled by Riyadh amid its fallout with Abu Dhabi.

David Cannon, the JNP’s chair, said the ban had been used against Jewish people speaking out for Palestine.

Deep inside the Tibesti mountains of northern Chad, in the central Sahara, the town of Miski sits surrounded by a succession of never-ending wadis.
A couple of families live at the top of each of these valleys and in August, when the rainy season comes, the wadis become a river that washes through the mountains. When the rains go, the valleys become green and camels feed on them.
A remote volcanic range characterised by rugged, bare rock, rivers of lava and volcanoes that climb to 3,000 metres, the Tibesti, which runs through northern Chad across the border into southern Libya, is sometimes called the roof of the Sahara.
These mountains are home to the Tubu, an indigenous community whose territory also includes a part of southern Libya, northern Niger and northwestern Sudan.

The mountains, too, are filled with antimony, a toxic heavy metal that is putting the ecosystem of this indigenous community at severe risk and is also exported in great quantities.
For decades, the gold that sits in this remote place has been one of the drivers of armed conflict between the Tubu and the Libyan then Chadian states.

The man, whose name was withheld for fear of reprisals, spent months in prison before video footage showed he had been nowhere near the scene of the crime he was accused of.

Amnesty says Palestinian women and girls bear crushing toll of Israel’s genocide
Amnesty International said on Wednesday that Israel continues to inflict devastating harm on Palestinian women and girls in Gaza as part of its ongoing genocide, despite the October 2025 ceasefire.
In a new 135-page report, the rights group documented the killing, maiming, forced displacement, unlawful detention and starvation of women and girls, as well as the deliberate denial of essential healthcare, including reproductive care, between October 2023 and October 2026.
“This new report sheds light on the profound gendered dimensions of Israel’s genocide, providing new details about the brutal harms inflicted on women and girls that continue to devastate their lives and cause agonizing suffering despite the so-called ceasefire,” said Agnes Callamard, Amnesty’s secretary general.
